segment_text: Let me set up the problem properly. Modern transformer models have many attention heads per layer, often sixteen or thirty-two. Each head learns to attend to different patterns. The question this paper asks is whether all of those heads are actually useful. The authors suspect that many of them learn redundant patterns, and that you could remove the redundant ones at inference time without changing the model's outputs much. To test this, they propose a scoring function that ranks heads by their contribution to the gradient flow during training.

segment_text: If you take the paper at face value, the implication is that we've been wasting compute by running every attention head on every input, when really only the top-ranked seventy percent matter for most queries, and the bottom thirty percent are essentially dead weight that you can safely skip, which if true would suggest similar ideas might work for feed-forward layers, mixture-of-experts gating, and other parts of the network that we currently treat as monolithic.
